content: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection is a liver disease caused by the hepatitis B virus, which can result in severe complications such as cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. Individuals with HBV infection may also have coinfections, including HIV or other hepatitis viruses like hepatitis C or D, which can increase the risk of death from any cause. Chronic HBV infection contributes to increased illness, psychological stress, and financial strain on affected individuals and their families. Radix Sophorae flavescentis, a type of herbal medicine, is often used in combination with other drugs or herbs. It is thought to alleviate symptoms and inhibit viral replication in people with chronic hepatitis B. However, the effects of Radix Sophorae flavescentis on outcomes that matter to patients remain unclear, and its widespread use has not been supported by rigorous scientific review. The objective of this study was to evaluate the benefits and harms of Radix Sophorae flavescentis compared to other drugs or herbs in individuals with chronic hepatitis B. To achieve this, researchers searched multiple databases, including The Cochrane Hepato-Biliary Group Controlled Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and others, up to December 2018. They also reviewed clinical trial registries for ongoing or unpublished studies. The study included randomized clinical trials that compared Radix Sophorae flavescentis to other drugs or herbs in people with chronic hepatitis B. Participants could also have had cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, or other coexisting conditions. Trials involving polyherbal mixtures containing Radix Sophorae flavescentis were excluded. Co-interventions were allowed if they were applied equally across all study groups. The primary outcomes assessed were all-cause mortality, serious adverse events, and health-related quality of life. Secondary outcomes included hepatitis B-related mortality, hepatitis B-related morbidity, and adverse events deemed not serious. The results were presented as risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). The risk of bias was evaluated using predefined criteria, and Trial Sequential Analyses were conducted to minimize random errors. The GRADE methodology was used to assess the certainty of the evidence. The review included 10 randomized clinical trials with a total of 898 participants. All trials were judged to have a high risk of bias. The interventions included oral capsules, intravenous infusions, intramuscular injections, and acupoint injections of Radix Sophorae flavescentis, with follow-up periods ranging from 1 to 12 months. The comparator drugs included lamivudine, adefovir, interferon, tiopronin, thymosin, and other Chinese herbs. Two trials included children up to 14 years old, and one trial involved participants with cirrhosis due to chronic hepatitis B. None of the trials reported data on all-cause mortality, health-related quality of life, serious adverse events, hepatitis B-related mortality, or hepatitis B-related morbidity. The evidence regarding whether Radix Sophorae flavescentis affects the occurrence of adverse events considered not serious was uncertain (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.42 to 1.75; I² = 0%; 2 trials, 163 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Similarly, it was unclear whether the intervention increased or decreased the proportion of participants with detectable HBV-DNA (RR 1.14, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.63; I² = 92%; 8 trials, 719 participants; very low-certainty evidence). However, Radix Sophorae flavescentis was associated with a reduction in the proportion of participants with detectable hepatitis B virus e-antigen (HBeAg) (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.75 to 0.98; I² = 43%; 7 trials, 588 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Two of the 10 trials were not funded, one received academic funding, and the remaining seven trials did not disclose funding information. The randomization process in an additional 109 trials was inadequately reported, preventing their inclusion in the review. The authors concluded that the included trials did not provide data on critical outcomes such as all-cause mortality, health-related quality of life, serious adverse events, hepatitis B-related mortality, or morbidity. The evidence regarding the effects of Radix Sophorae flavescentis on adverse events considered not serious and on detectable HBV-DNA remains unclear. While the intervention showed a reduction in detectable HBeAg, this result should be interpreted with caution due to the high risk of bias, the use of a non-validated surrogate outcome, and the very low certainty of the evidence. The lack of information on trial design for many studies and the potential influence of undisclosed funding raise concerns about the reliability of the findings. Given the widespread use of Radix Sophorae flavescentis, there is a need for large, unbiased, high-quality, placebo-controlled randomized trials that focus on patient-centered outcomes.
